title: 7 Best Home Generators for Power Outages (2026): Sized to Need
metaDescription: The Generac Guardian 22kW leads 7 outage generators; essentials alone need about 3,500 to 5,000 running watts, and a sump or well pump pushes that higher.
h1: Best Home Generator for Power Outages
keyword: best home generator for power outages
keywords: best home generator for power outages
intro:
The best home generator for power outages for most people in 2026 is the **[Generac Guardian 22kW](/gear/generac-guardian-22kw/)**. Where outages run long and often, nothing else on this list can stand in for an automatic standby unit.

Most houses need about 3,500 to 5,000 running watts for essentials, which a 7,000 to 9,500 watt dual fuel portable on an interlock covers with room to spare. Long, frequent outages, a well or sump pump, or central air push the answer toward the Generac Guardian 22kW standby. Below: seven picks, sizing math, safe hookup, carbon monoxide rules, fuel and real costs.

The right outage generator is the smallest machine that keeps your must-run loads going for as long as your outages really last, wired in through a transfer switch or interlock, and parked where its exhaust can never reach the house. Every section below builds on that idea.
quickAnswer: the Generac Guardian 22kW is our #1 pick (top pick: automatic whole-house). Where outages run long and often, nothing else on this list can stand in for an automatic standby unit.
picksHeading: The best home generators for power outages right now

picks.body: For a household that wants the power back without anyone stepping outside, the Guardian 22kW is the standard answer. It is mounted permanently on a pad, piped to natural gas or a propane tank and wired through an automatic transfer switch, so it detects the outage, starts and carries the house without help. Generac rates it at 22,000 watts on propane and 19,500 on natural gas, enough for a typical 2,000 to 3,000 square foot home with a central air conditioner and gas heat, particularly with the load-shedding modules Generac sells. The air-cooled engine runs a weekly self-exercise and reports its status to the Mobile Link app. The drawbacks are cost and paperwork: the unit alone is roughly $5,500 to $6,500 at the time of writing, and permits, electrical work, gas piping and the pad commonly bring the installed total to $10,000 to $18,000 or more. Budget for yearly oil, filter and plug service from a dealer.
pros: Starts and picks up the load by itself, usually within seconds of the grid failing
22kW on propane and 19.5kW on natural gas covers most homes, central air included
Runs for days on a natural gas line with no trips for fuel
Exercises itself weekly and reports over Wi-Fi through Generac's app
The largest dealer and service network of any standby brand
cons: Installed cost commonly runs well into five figures
Requires a permit, a concrete or composite pad and licensed trades
Yearly service is essential if you want it to start when it counts

picks.body: Most suburban homeowners should look at this portable first. The 9,200 figure is its peak starting rating on gasoline; running output is lower, and lower still on propane, so take the label's running-watt figure for each fuel when you build your load list. Even so, it sits in the class that can carry a refrigerator, a chest freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, Wi-Fi and a run of lights at once, with headroom for a window air conditioner if you stagger the start-ups. Dual fuel is worth more than the spec sheet implies: propane stores for years with no stabilizer, and after a hurricane or ice storm, a stack of filled cylinders is often easier to find than working gas pumps. Champion's CO Shield sensor shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide gathers around the unit. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,400 at the time of writing, plus a transfer switch or interlock fitted by an electrician.
pros: Burns gasoline or a standard propane cylinder, a real edge when gas stations are dark
Enough output to run a fridge, freezer, sump pump, furnace blower and lights together
Electric start with a recoil backup
Champion's CO Shield stops the engine if carbon monoxide builds up around it
A 120/240V locking outlet suits a manual transfer switch or interlock inlet
cons: Heavy enough that you will want the wheel kit and a helper
Loud next to an inverter; the neighbors will hear it
Produces less on propane than its gasoline rating

picks.body: The iGen4500 fills the gap many outage shoppers land in: more load than a small inverter can handle, but not the budget or patience for a 9,000-watt open frame. Westinghouse rates it at 3,700 running and 4,500 starting watts, which handles a refrigerator, a freezer, a gas furnace blower, a sump pump, lights and electronics as long as you are sensible about what runs at the same time. As an inverter, it makes power clean enough for sensitive electronics, and its engine throttles back at light load, which is where the long run time on a 3.4-gallon tank comes from. Owners commonly report it is clearly quieter than open-frame units of similar output, and remote start is a real comfort in a February storm. The limit is the 120V-only panel, which rules out a 240V well pump or an electric range. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: 3,700 running and 4,500 peak watts in a quiet inverter body
Clean inverter output suits electronics, furnace control boards and medical devices
Electric start plus a remote key fob
Long run time on its 3.4-gallon tank at light load
Onboard display shows load, fuel level and remaining run time
cons: 120V only, so a 240V well pump is out
Close to 100 pounds; you will use the wheels

picks.body: The EU2200i is the small inverter others are measured against, and the reasons are mostly unglamorous: it starts, it keeps starting, and dealer support for Honda engines is everywhere. Its ratings are 1,800 running and 2,200 starting watts, enough for a refrigerator plus lights, internet, phone charging and a TV, or a gas furnace blower by itself. Honda lists run time at about 3.2 hours at full rated load and about 8.1 hours at a quarter load on the 0.95-gallon tank, so build your fuel supply around those figures. Noise is rated at 48 to 57 dBA, which is why owners say they can run it near a neighbor's bedroom window without complaints. CO-MINDER stops the engine if carbon monoxide gathers nearby, a backup to good placement rather than a replacement for it. Two EU2200i units can be paralleled for more output. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: Honda GXR120 engine with a long reliability record
About 47 pounds, so one adult can genuinely carry it
Its 48 to 57 dBA rating is quiet enough for close neighbors
Can run in parallel with a second unit for double the output
CO-MINDER shuts it down automatically if carbon monoxide builds up
cons: 1,800 running watts restricts you to the essentials
An under-1-gallon tank means several refills a day at heavier loads
Priced noticeably above rival 2,200W inverters

picks.body: Choose the GP8000E when you want large portable output and are happy to run on gasoline. Generac rates it at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, enough for a 240V well pump, a refrigerator, a freezer, a furnace blower and lights through a transfer switch, or a window air conditioner in place of one of those. Electric start works from a key switch with a pull cord as backup, and the COsense module stops the engine if carbon monoxide gathers around it. The open frame and steel cradle are made to be hauled out of a shed, and the never-flat wheels help on gravel. Because it is a conventional generator rather than an inverter, the engine holds a fixed speed, so fuel burn and noise barely fall at light load. Set aside money for stabilized gasoline and approved cans. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts on gasoline
Electric start with a battery the generator keeps charged
COsense automatic carbon monoxide shutoff

A 120/240V locking outlet ready for a transfer switch

picks.body: The XP12000EH is close to the most generator most people would still call portable. DuroMax rates it at 12,000 starting and 9,500 running watts on gasoline, with lower figures on propane, and it has a 50-amp 120/240V outlet suited to a larger manual transfer switch or a panel interlock. That can run a central air conditioner in the smaller tonnage ranges alongside essentials, depending on its starting draw, or carry much of a house that has gas heat and a gas water heater. The compromises are physical. At well over 200 pounds it lives on its wheels, and at heavy load it burns many gallons of gasoline a day or needs a serious propane supply. If you are shopping at this size, get a price on a small standby unit as well; the gap shrinks once fuel, cans and labor are counted. Expect roughly $1,200 to $1,600 at the time of writing.

50-amp 120/240V outlet for a larger transfer switch or interlock

picks.body: The Delta Pro is a big lithium iron phosphate battery with an inverter, not a generator in the combustion sense, and that is precisely why it is here. With no engine, it can sit in a kitchen or bedroom running a refrigerator, a CPAP, a modem and lights with no carbon monoxide risk and no noise. EcoFlow rates the base unit at 3.6kWh of storage and 3,600 watts of continuous output, and extra battery packs expand the system. It recharges from a wall outlet, solar panels, a vehicle or EcoFlow's own smart gas generator, which turns it into a quiet buffer for a fuel-burning unit. The constraint is arithmetic: a typical refrigerator uses 1 to 2kWh a day, so one Delta Pro carries essentials for one to three days without solar. Expect roughly $2,500 to $3,500 at the time of writing, depending on bundles.

sections.heading: How Do Your Outages Decide Which Generator You Need?
sections.body:
The length of your longest recent outage, the season it hit and what stopped working decide the class of machine before any spec sheet does. Most generator regret comes from shopping for an imagined outage instead of the real one. A four-hour summer blackout and a six-day January ice storm need completely different equipment.

### How long and how often does your power go out?

Before reading a single listing, write down three things: how long your longest outage in the past five years lasted, what time of year it happened, and which failure genuinely hurt. Utilities publish reliability figures, but your own memory is usually good enough for this.

If your outages are short and rare, a small inverter or a battery power station keeps the refrigerator and internet going until the crews arrive. If they come often and stretch past a day, you need a fuel plan and enough output for heat or a sump pump, which points to a large portable with a transfer switch. If you have gone most of a week without power more than once, standby begins to make financial sense.

### What is the biggest load in your climate?

Climate sets your largest load. In the North, the furnace blower and its control board come first, and most gas furnaces draw only a few hundred watts. In the South, air conditioning is what makes an outage miserable, and a central unit is the single most expensive load to back up. A house on a private well adds a 240V pump to the list, and a house with a basement adds a sump pump that must not stop during a storm.

### Does anyone at home depend on power?

People change the list more than appliances do. Someone on oxygen, a CPAP, a refrigerated medication or a powered wheelchair reshuffles every priority. For those loads, silent battery power that is safe indoors is often the first thing to buy, with a fuel generator behind it to keep the battery topped up. Put your list on paper; the sizing section uses it.

THE SHORT VERSION

Pick the class from your outages, then the size from your load list.

Short and rare outages: a battery station or small inverter. Long, seasonal outages: a large portable with a transfer switch or interlock. Frequent multi-day outages, or someone at home who depends on power: automatic standby, often with a battery for medical loads.

sections.heading: Standby, Portable, Inverter or Battery: Which Type of Backup Is Best?
sections.body:
The class matters more than the brand: standby for long outages when nobody is home, conventional portables for watts per dollar, inverters for quiet essentials and batteries for indoor use. **Automatic standby** units are installed permanently outside, run on natural gas or propane and switch on by themselves. **Conventional portables** are open-frame engines on wheels that deliver a lot of watts for the money. **Inverter portables** make cleaner power more quietly and use little fuel at light load. **Battery stations** store energy instead of making it.

| Class | Typical output | Typical price | Best for | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic standby | 10-26kW | $10,000-$20,000 installed | Long, frequent outages; whole-house coverage | Cost, permits, annual service |
| Conventional portable | 5,000-12,000W | $700-$1,600 plus switch | Essentials or most of the house on a budget | Noise, fuel burn, manual setup |
| Inverter portable | 1,800-4,500W | $500-$1,300 | Quiet essentials, electronics, close neighbors | Limited output; most are 120V only |
| Battery station | 1-4kWh per unit | $400-$3,500 | Indoor use, medical devices, apartments | Runs out without solar or a generator |

### When is standby the right class?

Standby is the only class that works while nobody is home. That matters for a sump pump under a finished basement, for a freezer full of meat while you are on vacation, and for an elderly parent who should not be dragging a 200-pound machine across a wet lawn. On a natural gas line or a large propane tank, it is also the only class that never needs refueling.

### Conventional or inverter portable?

Conventional portables win on watts per dollar: an 8,000-watt open-frame unit costs about the same as a 4,500-watt inverter. You pay in noise and fuel. The engine runs at one fixed speed whether it is powering a refrigerator or a whole panel, so it burns gasoline at a similar rate either way. Inverter portables throttle down as demand falls, which is why a small inverter can run overnight on a tank while an open frame cannot.

### Where do battery stations fit?

Battery stations are the only option that is safe to run indoors. They shine in short outages, with overnight medical loads and in apartments, but their capacity is finite. A 1kWh station runs a modern refrigerator for most of a day, and a 3.6kWh unit buys a couple of days of essentials. Pair one with solar or a small inverter generator outside and you have a quiet, efficient hybrid. Our [portable power station rankings](/best-portable-power-station/) dig into capacity and chemistry. For a circuit-by-circuit outage plan built around batteries, read our guide to the [best power stations for home backup](/best-portable-power-station-for-home-backup/), and for recharging off the grid, see our [solar generator pairings](/best-solar-generator/).

sections.heading: How Many Watts Do You Need to Run a House During an Outage?
sections.body:
About 3,500 to 5,000 running watts covers the essentials, a sump or 240V well pump pushes that toward 6,000 to 8,000, and most whole homes with central air need 20kW or more. Your own number comes from a load list built on running watts, with the biggest starting surge checked on top.

### What is the difference between running and starting watts?

Any appliance with a motor needs a burst of extra power to get going, often two to three times its running draw for a second or two, which is why generators carry two ratings. **Running watts** are what the machine can supply without a break. **Starting watts**, also called peak or surge watts, are the short overload it can absorb while a compressor or pump spins up. Size the generator against running watts, then confirm that your single largest motor can start on top of everything else that is running.

| Load | Typical running watts | Typical starting watts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Refrigerator (modern) | 150-800 | 1,200-2,200 |
| Chest freezer | 100-500 | 800-1,500 |
| Sump pump, 1/3 to 1/2 hp | 800-1,050 | 1,300-2,200 |
| Well pump, 1/2 to 1 hp (240V) | 1,000-2,000 | 2,000-4,000 |
| Gas furnace blower, 1/3 to 1/2 hp | 300-800 | 1,000-2,300 |
| Window AC, 10,000 BTU | 900-1,200 | 1,500-2,200 |
| Central AC, 3 ton | 3,000-4,000 | Often 8,000+ without a soft starter |
| Microwave | 1,000-1,500 | Same as running |
| LED lights, modem, router, TV, phones | 200-400 total | Same as running |

### How do you find your own appliance numbers?

The table shows typical ranges, not your figures. The real numbers sit on each appliance's data plate, usually in amps: multiply amps by 120 for most household loads, or by 240 for a well pump or a central air condenser. A clamp meter on the circuit reads the running draw directly. Older refrigerators and pumps often draw more than the table suggests, and a worn compressor can need considerably more to start.

### What does a worked example look like?

Take a common Midwest house with gas heat and a basement: refrigerator 700, freezer 400, sump pump 1,000, furnace blower 600, lights and internet 400, and a microwave used now and then at 1,200. That is about 4,300 running watts. The largest starting surge belongs to the sump pump at about 2,200, so if everything kicks on together, peak demand is roughly 5,500 watts. A portable with 7,000 to 8,000 running watts covers that comfortably, while a 3,700-watt inverter covers it only if the microwave waits.

Sizing Rules of Thumb

2,000W

Fridge, lights, phones, internet

5,000W

Plus sump, furnace blower, freezer

8,000W

Plus a 240V well pump or window AC

20kW+

Most whole homes with central air

### How much headroom should you leave?

Keep roughly 20 percent in reserve. Generators run hotter, louder and less efficiently near their limit, and voltage sag under heavy load can strain motors. If your list comes to 7,500 running watts, a 9,000-watt machine is the honest choice. If central air is what makes the number huge, ask an HVAC technician about a soft-start kit, which can cut a compressor's starting surge substantially and sometimes lets a large portable or a smaller standby unit carry it.

sections.heading: How Do You Safely Connect a Generator to Your House?
sections.body:
There are exactly three safe ways to bring generator power into a home. The first is heavy-duty outdoor extension cords run from the generator straight to individual appliances. The second is a **manual transfer switch** installed beside your panel by an electrician, with a power inlet box outside. The third is a listed **interlock kit** fitted to your main panel by an electrician, again with an inlet. Standby units use an automatic transfer switch that does the same job without anyone touching it.

NEVER BACKFEED

Never plug a generator into a wall outlet or a dryer receptacle.

A cord with a male plug on both ends, sometimes called a suicide cord, pushes generator power backward through your panel and out onto the utility lines, where the pole transformer steps it up to thousands of volts. Line workers fixing what they believe is a dead line can be electrocuted, and neighbors can be injured. It also energizes your house wiring with no main breaker protection and can start a fire when grid power comes back. It breaks the National Electrical Code and is illegal in most jurisdictions.

### Why does a transfer switch or interlock matter?

Every legal connection shares one feature: isolation. A transfer switch or interlock physically guarantees that the house is fed by the utility or by the generator, never both at the same moment. That protects line crews, protects the generator from destruction when the grid returns, and protects your wiring. It is not an optional extra; it is what lets a portable safely run hardwired loads like a furnace or a well pump, which extension cords cannot reach.

### What does a transfer switch or interlock cost?

Prices vary by region. A manual transfer switch covering six to ten chosen circuits, plus an outdoor inlet and a permit, commonly costs $800 to $1,800 installed. An interlock kit is cheaper, often $500 to $1,200 installed, and lets you power any circuit in the panel provided you manage the load yourself. Most places require a permit for either, and both belong in the hands of a licensed electrician. Match the inlet to the generator: a 30-amp L14-30 suits most mid-size portables, and the largest need a 50-amp inlet.

### How do you use extension cords safely?

Choose outdoor-rated cords of 12-gauge or heavier, sized for the load, and keep them as short as you practically can. Never route them through a door or window that then has to stay propped open, because that gap is exactly where exhaust gets in; a cord port in an exterior wall or a properly installed inlet is the better answer. Newer portables with GFCI-protected outlets sometimes trip when connected through a transfer switch. That is a neutral-bonding issue for your electrician to sort out, not a reason to defeat the protection. A [whole-house surge protector](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/) is worth adding during the same visit, and a circuit breaker finder speeds up choosing the right circuits for a transfer switch.

sections.heading: How Do You Prevent Carbon Monoxide Poisoning From a Generator?
sections.body:
Run a fuel-burning generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house with the exhaust aimed away, and back that up with battery-powered CO alarms and a generator that has an automatic CO shutoff. Portable generators are among the leading causes of carbon monoxide deaths in the United States, and most of those deaths happen during and just after storms. One portable generator can produce as much carbon monoxide as hundreds of idling cars. The gas has no color or smell, and early symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea and fatigue are easily mistaken for flu or exhaustion. People who are asleep can die without ever waking up.

### Where can a generator run, and where can it never run?

The rules are short and absolute. A fuel-burning generator runs outdoors and nowhere else: not in the house, a basement, a crawlspace, an attached garage, a breezeway or a shed, and not in a garage with the door up, because fans and open doors do not clear the gas reliably. Federal safety agencies recommend at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows and vents. More distance is better and wind direction matters; the research behind that guidance shows exhaust can still drift inside at 20 feet in the wrong conditions.

Placement Numbers to Remember

0

Safe indoor locations for an engine

20 ft+

Portable to house, exhaust pointed away

5 ft

Typical standby clearance to windows and vents

Every level

Battery-backed CO alarms, near bedrooms

### Which CO alarms work in an outage?

Only alarms that do not rely on grid power: battery-only units, or plug-ins with a battery backup, placed on every level and outside every sleeping area. Test them before storm season starts. If an alarm goes off or anyone feels ill, get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911. Do not go back inside to hunt for the source.

### Does an automatic CO shutoff make a generator safe?

It makes it safer, so buy one that has it. Honda calls the feature CO-MINDER, Champion uses CO Shield, Generac uses COsense, and other brands have their own names; the usual reference standards are ANSI/PGMA G300 and UL 2201. These systems stop the engine when CO builds up around the unit, which guards against the most common fatal error, running in a garage or too close to the house. They are a backstop, not permission to cut corners on placement. Standby generators are installed to the maker's clearance rules, commonly 5 feet from openings, and inspected under a permit, one more reason they are the safest fuel-burning choice.

### What do you do when it rains?

Weather is the trap, because rain is what tempts people to move a generator into the garage. Instead, buy a purpose-made generator tent or a ventilated enclosure rated for use while running, or build a simple open-sided canopy well away from the house. And never refuel a hot engine: let it cool first so gasoline cannot spill onto a hot muffler.

sections.heading: How Much Fuel Should You Store for a Generator?
sections.body:
Store enough for three days of intermittent running, which for a mid-size portable is usually 15 to 25 gallons of stabilized gasoline or several propane cylinders. Fuel is what runs out first in a regional outage: gas stations need electricity to pump, and the ones that have it draw long lines. Plan for your longest likely outage at a realistic load, not the brochure run time at 25 percent load.

### How fast does a generator burn fuel?

Mid-size conventional portables commonly use somewhere around half a gallon to a gallon of gasoline an hour at moderate load, which adds up to 12 to 24 gallons a day if they run around the clock. Most owners do not run them that way. Running the generator for two hours out of every four to six keeps a refrigerator and freezer cold and a sump pit in check while cutting fuel use dramatically. A small inverter at light load can run all night on a single gallon.

### How long does stored gasoline last?

Not long. Untreated pump gas starts to break down within a month or two, and ethanol blends pull in water. Add stabilizer when you fill the can, rotate the stored fuel into your car every few months, and buy ethanol-free gas if you can find it nearby. Keep it in approved containers in a detached shed or garage, away from ignition sources and never in the living space. Local fire codes often limit household gasoline storage, commonly to around 25 gallons, so check the rule where you live.

### Is propane or natural gas easier?

Propane is far easier to stockpile. It does not go stale, standard 20-pound cylinders are sold at hardware stores, and a dual fuel portable lets you switch over when gasoline gets scarce. Expect about 10 percent less output on propane, and be aware that small cylinders can struggle to vaporize fast enough under heavy load in deep cold. Natural gas, which most standby units burn, rarely fails during electrical outages, which is why a gas-fed standby can keep running for days.

RULE OF THUMB

Keep three days of fuel for intermittent running.

For a mid-size portable run two hours on and four hours off, that usually means 15 to 25 gallons of stabilized gasoline or several propane cylinders. If your outages regularly outlast that supply, the numbers are pointing you toward a standby unit on natural gas or a large propane tank.

sections.heading: How Much Does a Home Generator Really Cost?
sections.body:
A $1,200 portable becomes a $2,500 to $3,500 system once it is connected and equipped, and a whole-home 20 to 24kW standby unit commonly lands between $10,000 and $20,000 installed. Once connection, fuel and upkeep are counted, the sticker price is the smallest number in the decision.

### What does a portable system cost?

The portable is only the start. Add an inlet with a transfer switch or interlock and a permit, a heavy cord, fuel cans, stabilizer, a cover and better CO alarms, and the total reaches that $2,500 to $3,500 range. That is still far below standby, and for most homes with gas heat it is the best value on this list.

### What does standby cost installed?

Standby works on a different scale. The unit itself is roughly a third to a half of the bill; the rest covers the automatic transfer switch, electrical work, gas piping and sometimes a bigger gas meter, the pad, permits and inspection. Long gas runs, propane tank sets and electrical service upgrades push the total above the usual $10,000 to $20,000 range. Our [Generac cost breakdown](/generac-generator-cost/) goes through each line of a typical quote.

### What does it cost to keep running?

Standby units need a service visit every year, typically $200 to $400 on a dealer plan, plus a new battery every few years, and their weekly self-exercise burns a small amount of fuel. Portables need an oil change after the first few hours and then on a schedule tied to run hours, along with plugs and air filters. The fuel you rotate into your car is not really wasted.

### Is a generator worth the money?

Set the cost against what an outage costs you. A flooded finished basement can cost more than a standby installation, and a freezer of meat, a week in a hotel, lost remote-work income or a burst frozen pipe are all real money. If two or three of those events have hit you in the past five years, a generator is not a luxury. If your outages are four hours once a summer, a battery station and a cooler are the rational answer.

sections.heading: How Do You Keep a Generator Ready for an Outage?
sections.body:
Follow a routine: run it monthly, manage the fuel, service it on schedule and rehearse the hookup before storm season. The most common generator failure is not mechanical at all. It is a machine that sat for a year with old fuel in the carburetor, where varnish from evaporated gasoline clogs the tiny passages of a small engine, so the unit that started fine in the store will not start in a storm.

### For portables

Start it once a month and run it for 15 to 20 minutes with a real load plugged in, such as a space heater or a work light. Either keep stabilized fuel in the tank or run the carburetor dry with the fuel valve closed before storage, whichever the manual recommends for your model. Change the oil after the break-in period the manual specifies and then by run hours, and check the level before every outage. If the unit does not charge its own electric-start battery, keep that battery on a maintainer.

### For standby units

Let the weekly exercise cycle run and watch the app or controller for warnings. Book a yearly service that covers oil, filters, plugs, a battery test and a transfer switch check. Keep mulch, snow drifts, shrubs and leaves clear of the enclosure so the cooling air intake can breathe. After any long outage, have the oil checked, because a multi-day run eats a large part of the service interval.

### Do a dry run before storm season

Roll the portable out, connect it through the inlet, flip the interlock or transfer switch and bring the circuits on one at a time. That is how you discover the missing adapter, the dead battery or the cord that is too short on a sunny afternoon instead of at midnight in the rain. Keep a printed card by the panel listing the steps in order, and teach a second adult in the house to do it.

sections.heading: Which Generator Is Best for Your Type of Home?
sections.body:
Match the pick to the house and the people in it. These five situations cover most homes, and each points to a different machine on the list.

### Suburban house with gas heat and a basement

If multi-day outages come along now and then, the Champion dual fuel or the Generac GP8000E on an interlock or manual transfer switch covers the sump pump, furnace, refrigerator and freezer. This is the most common situation, and it is where the best value on the list sits.

### Rural house on a well with long outages

The pump needs 240V, so a 120V-only inverter cannot be the main unit. The GP8000E or the DuroMax handles the pump, and the DuroMax has enough left for a window air conditioner. If you lose power for most of a week every year, get a price on the Guardian 22kW running from a propane tank. Small cabins and lighter loads are covered in our guide to the [best small generators for home](/best-small-generator-for-home/).

### Southern home where heat is the danger

Central air dominates the load here, so the honest options are standby with load management, or a large portable with a soft-start kit on the condenser. A window unit in one bedroom, run from a mid-size portable, is a cheaper middle route that keeps people safe through a heat wave.

### Apartment, condo or a medical device at home

Start with the EcoFlow Delta Pro or a smaller battery station. It runs safely indoors, and if outages drag on you can add a quiet inverter outside to recharge it.

### Close neighbors and short outages

The Honda EU2200i or the Westinghouse iGen4500 keeps the essentials running without much noise. If you would rather have plain gasoline and big output, compare our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) picks.

mistakes.title: Buying by the big number on the box
mistakes.body: The headline figure on most packaging is starting watts, not what the machine can sustain all night. Build your list from running watts, add the largest single starting surge, and keep about 20 percent headroom. A generator held at its limit for hours wears quickly and sags voltage in ways motors dislike.

mistakes.title: Leaving out the transfer switch
mistakes.body: Extension cords handle a fridge and a lamp, but they cannot reach a furnace, a well pump or a hardwired sump pump. Plugging into a wall outlet to power those backfeeds the grid and can kill a line worker. Count an interlock or transfer switch, installed under a permit, as part of the generator's price.

mistakes.title: Running it in the garage to keep it dry
mistakes.body: Every storm season brings deaths from generators run in attached garages with the door open, because the gas reaches the house faster than people expect. Keep it outdoors, 20 feet or more from the house with the exhaust aimed away, under a ventilated cover in rain, and keep battery CO alarms working.

mistakes.title: Storing it with stale gasoline
mistakes.body: Untreated fuel left in the tank for a year varnishes the carburetor, and the generator refuses to start when you need it. Add stabilizer every time you fill a can, run the unit monthly under load, and either keep the tank stabilized or run the carburetor dry as the manual directs.

mistakes.title: Buying more generator than you can fuel
mistakes.body: At heavy load a 12,000-watt portable can go through a lot of gasoline in a day, and stations shut down in regional outages. Before buying big, work out where three days of fuel will come from. If you cannot answer that, a smaller unit run in cycles, propane, or a natural gas standby is the better plan.

faqs.q: How big a generator do I need for an average house during an outage?
faqs.a: Essentials alone, meaning a refrigerator, freezer, lights, internet and a gas furnace blower, need about 3,500 to 5,000 running watts. A sump pump or a 240V well pump moves you into the 6,000 to 8,000 watt range. Central air plus the whole panel usually takes a 20 to 24kW standby unit or a smaller one with load management. Read your appliance data plates instead of trusting averages.

faqs.q: Is a standby generator worth it over a good portable?
faqs.a: That turns on how often and how long your power goes out. Standby costs several times as much, but it starts itself, needs no refueling on natural gas and covers the whole house. Multi-day outages most years, a finished basement, or someone at home who cannot manage a portable usually justify it. For occasional outages, a portable with an interlock is much better value.

faqs.q: How far from the house should a portable generator be?
faqs.a: Federal safety guidance calls for at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust aimed away from doors, windows and vents, and more distance is better. Never run one in a garage, a carport against the house, a basement, a crawlspace or a shed, even with the doors open. Back up good placement with a CO shutoff generator and battery-powered CO alarms on every level.

faqs.q: Can I plug my generator into a dryer outlet to power the house?
faqs.a: No. That is backfeeding, and it can electrocute utility workers, hurt neighbors, wreck your generator when grid power returns and start a fire. It also breaks electrical code. The legal routes to house circuits are a manual transfer switch or a listed panel interlock with an outdoor inlet, installed by a licensed electrician, or extension cords run straight to appliances.

faqs.q: Will a portable generator run my central air conditioner?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A 3-ton condenser usually runs on 3,000 to 4,000 watts but can need several times that to start. A large portable in the 9,000-plus running watt class can often manage it, especially with a soft-start kit fitted by an HVAC technician, though little may be left for anything else. Many households cool one room with a window unit instead.

faqs.q: How long will a generator run on a tank of gas?
faqs.a: Load decides it. A small inverter can run eight hours or more at light load on about a gallon, while a large open-frame portable might manage eight to twelve hours at half load on a big tank and much less near full load. Look up the manufacturer's run-time figures at 25 and 50 percent load and plan your fuel around realistic use.

faqs.q: Is a battery power station a real replacement for a generator?
faqs.a: For short outages, apartments and medical devices, yes, and it is the only backup you can run indoors. For multi-day outages it supplements a generator rather than replacing one, unless solar panels or a generator recharge it. A typical refrigerator uses 1 to 2 kWh a day, so divide the station's capacity by your daily loads to estimate how long it lasts.

bottomLine:
For most houses the best outage generator is a dual fuel portable in the 7,000 to 9,500 running-watt range, wired in through an interlock or transfer switch and backed by a fuel plan for three days. Where outages are long, frequent or a danger to the people at home, a **[Generac Guardian 22kW](/gear/generac-guardian-22kw/)** standby unit is the investment that solves the problem for good.

Two rules hold whatever you buy: the engine runs outdoors, well clear of the house, with battery CO alarms inside, and it connects to your wiring only through a proper transfer switch or interlock. Get those two right and any machine on this list will do its job.
